title: Which Android Apps Can Use Your Camera, Mic and Location
html:
Android keeps a record of which apps used your camera, microphone and location, and it lets you switch each one off. The Privacy dashboard shows you what happened. The Permission manager lets you change it, one permission at a time. And Android can clean up after apps you have stopped using. Start there, then decide which apps are not worth keeping.

Last updated: 10 Oct 2026. Menu names differ a little between brands and Android versions; if you cannot find one, type its name into the Settings search box.

I opened the Privacy dashboard and Permission manager on a vivo V23 Pro running Android 14 (Funtouch OS 14, security update January 2025) on 10 Oct 2026. The dashboard showed the past 24 hours: Location used by 3 apps, Camera by 4 and Microphone by 2. Permission manager showed, for example, Location allowed for 31 of 52 apps and Microphone for 17 of 56.

See what apps have already done: the Privacy dashboard

Open Settings, then Security and privacy (or just Privacy), then Privacy dashboard. Pick a permission such as Camera, Microphone or Location and you will see which apps used it and when. Tap an app in that list to change its permission right there. Google says the dashboard covers the last 7 days on Android 13 and newer, and the last 24 hours on Android 12. How far back it goes depends on the phone: on my vivo V23 Pro (Android 14) the screen said "Past 24 hours".

Look for an app that used the microphone or location when you were not using it. That is not proof of anything bad (a navigation app or a voice recorder has a reason), but it tells you where to look next.

See what is happening right now: the green indicator

On Android 12 and newer, a green indicator appears at the top right of the screen when an app is using the camera or the microphone. Swipe down and tap it to see which app. You can also swipe down twice to open Quick Settings and switch the camera and microphone tiles off for the whole phone.

Change permissions: by app, or by permission

  • For one app: Settings, then Apps, pick the app, then Permissions.
  • For one permission across all apps: Settings, then Security and privacy, then Privacy, then Permission manager. Pick Camera, say, and see every app that has it.
  • Phone-wide switch: on phones that have it, Settings, then Security and privacy, then Privacy, then Privacy controls lets you turn off Camera access or Microphone access for all apps.

For location, camera and microphone you can choose "Allow only while using the app", "Ask every time" or "Don't allow". Location also has "All the time". "Only while using the app" is enough for most apps. If an app stops working properly after you remove a permission, you can give it back.

Let Android take permissions back from apps you forgot

Open Settings, then Apps, then Unused apps. For apps you have not opened for a long time, Android deletes temporary files, takes back permissions, stops them from running in the background and stops their notifications. To keep one app out of this, open its App info, go to Unused apps and turn off "Pause app activity if unused".

Ask one question about every permission

Does the permission match what the app does? A photo editor asking for the camera is normal. A flashlight or a calculator asking for contacts or location is a reason to say no. Android will tell the app you refused, and a well-made app keeps working without it.

One more setting is worth a look: Settings, then Apps, then Special app access, then Install unknown apps. It shows which apps are allowed to install other apps from outside the Play Store. Most people should see none, or only their file manager or browser if they chose to allow it.

How to decide which apps to delete

A list of "apps to delete" goes out of date quickly and can be wrong for your phone. These checks work on any app you are unsure about.

  1. Check what it costs you. In Settings, look at Battery usage and Data usage. An app you hardly open that sits near the top is a candidate.
  2. Read the Data safety section. On the app's Play Store page, scroll to Data safety and tap See details. It shows what data the app says it collects and shares. Remember that developers write this section themselves, and Google's own page says that a security review does not verify its accuracy.
  3. Look up its trackers. Exodus Privacy, a French non-profit, publishes reports that list the trackers and permissions inside Android apps. Search for the app at reports.exodus-privacy.eu.org.
  4. Remove one app, then compare. Check your storage or battery number again a day later.

If the app is a loan app, check it before you share anything. Under the RBI's Digital Lending Directions, 2025, regulated lenders must report the digital lending apps they use to the RBI, and that data is published on the RBI website. If an app says it works with a bank or NBFC and it is not listed there, do not give it your documents or contacts.

An example: Instagram on my phone

I ran these checks on Instagram on my vivo V23 Pro on 11 Oct 2026. In Battery, Instagram was at the top of the Power consumption rankings. In Data usage it showed 16.86 GB for the month on my phone: 16.30 GB in the foreground and 578 MB in the background.

Its App permissions screen has Camera, Microphone, Notifications and Photos and videos set to Allowed, Location set to Ask every time, and Calendar, Contacts, Nearby devices and Phone set to Not allowed.

On its Play Store page, the Data safety section says the app may share Personal info and Device or other IDs with third parties, may collect Location, Personal info and 12 other data types, encrypts data in transit, and offers account deletion.

The Exodus Privacy report I read for Instagram (version 450.0.0.50.77 from Google Play, report created 10 Oct 2026) lists 4 trackers: Facebook Flipper, Facebook Login, Facebook Notifications and Google Analytics, and 76 permissions. Exodus lists what is declared in the app's code, so many of those permissions are ones I have not granted on my phone.

My decision: I am keeping Instagram and leaving these permission settings as they are.

What to do next

  1. Open the Privacy dashboard and read what it shows for Camera, Microphone and Location.
  2. Set most apps to "Allow only while using the app", and switch off permissions that do not match what the app does.
  3. Keep "Pause app activity if unused" on for apps you rarely open.
  4. If you think an app is doing something it should not, see our guides on Google Play Protect and Safe mode.
